**SANRAL** (officially the **South African National Roads Agency SOC Ltd**) is a [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa")[parastatal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parastatal "Parastatal") responsible for the management, maintenance, and development of South Africa's national road network.

The network includes many of the country's [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Route_(South_Africa) "National Route (South Africa)") ("N") roadways, as well as some of its [Provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_routes_(South_Africa) "Provincial routes (South Africa)") and [Regional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_routes_(South_Africa) "Regional routes (South Africa)") ("R") ones.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-sanralRolePlayers-3)

SANRAL reports to the [Department of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Department of Transport (South Africa)"), headed by the [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Minister of Transport (South Africa)"). SANRAL works alongside similar agencies, such as [PRASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRASA "PRASA"), [ACSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Company_South_Africa "Airports Company South Africa"), and the [RTMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_Traffic_Management_Corporation "Road Traffic Management Corporation").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

SANRAL was created by _The South African National Roads Agency Limited and National Roads Act, 1998_ as a [corporatized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporatization "Corporatization") successor to the South African Roads Board, which was part of the [Department of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Department of Transport (South Africa)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-4) It was registered as a [public limited company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_limited_company "Public limited company") on 19 May 1998.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-cipro-5)

In 2011, SANRAL became the target of popular resentment, as tolling was about to commence on many of SANRAL's freeways in Gauteng, in order to finance their soon to be completed expansions, as part of the first phase of the Gauteng Freeway Improvement Project.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-7)

The GFIP was instituted to deal with the severe traffic congestion on [Gauteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng "Gauteng")'s freeways.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-8) The applicable Gauteng freeways were declared as [e-toll highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-toll_(Gauteng) "E-toll (Gauteng)") and they began [open road tolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_road_tolling "Open road tolling") on 3 December 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-9) E-tolls were discontinued on 12 April 2024.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-11)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Governance")]

SANRAL's only shareholder is the state, represented by the [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Minister of Transport (South Africa)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-12) The agency is governed by an eight-member [Board of Directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Directors "Board of Directors"). Five voting members–the [chairperson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson "Chairperson") and four others–are appointed by the Minister of Transport for a term of three years.

Two government officials are non-voting members, one from the Department of Transport and nominated by the Minister of Transport, and the other from the [National Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Treasury_(South_Africa) "National Treasury (South Africa)") and nominated by the [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(South_Africa) "Minister of Finance (South Africa)"). The [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer"), who is appointed by the Minister of Transport on the recommendation of the Board, is _[ex officio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex\_officio "Ex officio")_ a non-voting member of the Board.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-13)

## Operations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Operations")]

SANRAL operates a head office and four regional offices; Northern Region ([Gauteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng "Gauteng"), [North West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_(South_African_province) "North West (South African province)"), [Limpopo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limpopo "Limpopo") and [Mpumalanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpumalanga "Mpumalanga")); Western Region ([Western Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Cape "Western Cape") and [Northern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Cape "Northern Cape")); Eastern Region ([Free State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_State_(South_African_province) "Free State (South African province)") and [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu-Natal "KwaZulu-Natal")); and Southern Region ([Eastern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Cape "Eastern Cape")).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-14) In 2009 the agency managed a total of 16,170 kilometres of roads,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-ar-1):14 and by 2014, more than 22,000 kilometers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-citizen-15)

SANRAL's operations are divided into two broad categories, namely toll roads, which are self-funding, and non-toll roads, which are funded by transfers from the Department of Transport. In 2014 toll roads constituted 14% (c. 3,000 km) of its responsibilities, and non-toll roads 86% (c. 19,000 km).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-citizen-15)

Some toll roads are concessions, privately funded and managed with supervision from SANRAL; these include the [Platinum Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Highway "Platinum Highway") ([N1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N1_road_(South_Africa) "N1 road (South Africa)")/[N4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N4_road_(South_Africa) "N4 road (South Africa)")), the [Maputo Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maputo_Corridor "Maputo Corridor") (N4) and the [N3 Toll Concession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N3_(South_Africa)#N3_Toll_Concession "N3 (South Africa)").

Other toll roads are owned and operated directly by SANRAL; these include the [Huguenot Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot_Tunnel "Huguenot Tunnel") (N1), the [Tsitsikamma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsitsikamma "Tsitsikamma") Toll Road (N2), the [N2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N2_road_(South_Africa) "N2 road (South Africa)") tolls on the KwaZulu-Natal coast, the [Mariannhill Toll Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariannhill_Toll_Road "Mariannhill Toll Road") (N3), the N1 tolls in the Free State, Gauteng and Limpopo and the [N17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N17_(South_Africa) "N17 (South Africa)") tolls in Gauteng and Mpumalanga. It also owns and operates a tollgate on a provincial route (and not a national route), namely the Brandfort Toll Plaza on the R30 section of the [R30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R30_(South_Africa) "R30 (South Africa)")/[R730](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R730_(South_Africa) "R730 (South Africa)")/[R34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R34_(South_Africa) "R34 (South Africa)") ZR Mahabane Highway north of [Bloemfontein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloemfontein "Bloemfontein"). It also owns and operates the two tollgates on the [M4 freeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_(Pretoria) "M4 (Pretoria)") (Magalies Toll Route) west of Pretoria in Gauteng.

## Contributions to palaeontology and modern science

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Contributions to palaeontology and modern science")]

See also: [Waterloo Farm lagerstätte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Farm_lagerst%C3%A4tte "Waterloo Farm lagerstätte")

In the mid-1980s, a road bypass was constructed around Grahamstown (now [Makhanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makhanda,_Eastern_Cape "Makhanda, Eastern Cape")), to prevent traffic between [Port Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Elizabeth "Port Elizabeth") and [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London,_Eastern_Cape "East London, Eastern Cape") from driving through the [townships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Township_(South_Africa) "Township (South Africa)") following [Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") uprisings (which were progressively getting more heated at the time), making it unsafe for motorists.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-16) In 1999 the newly constituted SANRAL tendered for upgrades of an unstable road cutting along this route. This road cutting contained an important 360 million year old fossil site previously researched by Robert W. Gess.

In 1999, SANRAL teamed up with Gess to assist with salvage blocks of a black shale from the cutting to prevent their loss to science. This and further salvage of shale blocks during further work on the cutting by SANRAL contractees in 2007–2008, and their subsequent ongoing excavation, led to the revelation of the now world renowned Waterloo Farm lagerstätte, the only estuarine fossil site in the world from about 360 million years ago, with exceptional soft-tissue preservation.

A few of the note-worthy fossils from Waterloo Farm include those of the first four-legged creatures (tetrapods) from Africa – _[Tutusius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutusius "Tutusius") umlambo_ and _[Umzantsia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umzantsia "Umzantsia") amazana_, as well as many other vertebrates such as Placodermi (e.g., _[Bothriolepis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bothriolepis "Bothriolepis") africana_; _[Groenlandaspis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groenlandaspis "Groenlandaspis") riniensi_), Acanthodii (e.g., _[Diplacanthus acus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplacanthus\_acus "Diplacanthus acus")_), Chondrichthyes (e.g., _[Antarctilamna ultima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctilamna\_ultima "Antarctilamna ultima")_), Actinopterygii and Sarcopterigii (e.g., _[Serenichthys kowiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenichthys\_kowiensis "Serenichthys kowiensis")_).

Agnatha included the worlds oldest fossil lamprey (_Priscomyzon riniensis_), the recently described juvenile which overturned our assumptions about vertebrates ancestry. The site has also revealed invertebrate remains including the scorpion _[Gondwanascorpio emzantsiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwanascorpio\_emzantsiensis "Gondwanascorpio emzantsiensis")_, the oldest land animal from [Gondwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwana "Gondwana"), and a diverse flora of plants including _[Archaeopteris notosaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeopteris\_notosaria "Archaeopteris notosaria")_, Africa's earliest woody tree. In addition to numerus undescribed taxa and those currently being described (Housed at the Devonian Ecosystems Lab, Albany Museum, Makhanda), Gess and his team still has decade's worth of work ahead from the excavated blocks that were rescued from the road works with the help of SANRAL.

**SANRAL** (officially the **South African National Roads Agency SOC Ltd**) is a [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa")[parastatal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parastatal "Parastatal") responsible for the management, maintenance, and development of South Africa's national road network.

The network includes many of the country's [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Route_(South_Africa) "National Route (South Africa)") ("N") roadways, as well as some of its [Provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_routes_(South_Africa) "Provincial routes (South Africa)") and [Regional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_routes_(South_Africa) "Regional routes (South Africa)") ("R") ones.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-sanralRolePlayers-3)

SANRAL reports to the [Department of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Department of Transport (South Africa)"), headed by the [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Minister of Transport (South Africa)"). SANRAL works alongside similar agencies, such as [PRASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRASA "PRASA"), [ACSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Company_South_Africa "Airports Company South Africa"), and the [RTMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_Traffic_Management_Corporation "Road Traffic Management Corporation").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

SANRAL was created by _The South African National Roads Agency Limited and National Roads Act, 1998_ as a [corporatized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporatization "Corporatization") successor to the South African Roads Board, which was part of the [Department of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Department of Transport (South Africa)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-4) It was registered as a [public limited company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_limited_company "Public limited company") on 19 May 1998.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-cipro-5)

In 2011, SANRAL became the target of popular resentment, as tolling was about to commence on many of SANRAL's freeways in Gauteng, in order to finance their soon to be completed expansions, as part of the first phase of the Gauteng Freeway Improvement Project.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-7)

The GFIP was instituted to deal with the severe traffic congestion on [Gauteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng "Gauteng")'s freeways.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-8) The applicable Gauteng freeways were declared as [e-toll highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-toll_(Gauteng) "E-toll (Gauteng)") and they began [open road tolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_road_tolling "Open road tolling") on 3 December 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-9) E-tolls were discontinued on 12 April 2024.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-11)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Governance")]

SANRAL's only shareholder is the state, represented by the [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(South_Africa) "Minister of Transport (South Africa)").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-12) The agency is governed by an eight-member [Board of Directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Directors "Board of Directors"). Five voting members–the [chairperson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson "Chairperson") and four others–are appointed by the Minister of Transport for a term of three years.

Two government officials are non-voting members, one from the Department of Transport and nominated by the Minister of Transport, and the other from the [National Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Treasury_(South_Africa) "National Treasury (South Africa)") and nominated by the [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(South_Africa) "Minister of Finance (South Africa)"). The [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer"), who is appointed by the Minister of Transport on the recommendation of the Board, is _[ex officio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex\_officio "Ex officio")_ a non-voting member of the Board.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-13)

## Operations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Operations")]

SANRAL operates a head office and four regional offices; Northern Region ([Gauteng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng "Gauteng"), [North West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_(South_African_province) "North West (South African province)"), [Limpopo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limpopo "Limpopo") and [Mpumalanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpumalanga "Mpumalanga")); Western Region ([Western Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Cape "Western Cape") and [Northern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Cape "Northern Cape")); Eastern Region ([Free State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_State_(South_African_province) "Free State (South African province)") and [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu-Natal "KwaZulu-Natal")); and Southern Region ([Eastern Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Cape "Eastern Cape")).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-14) In 2009 the agency managed a total of 16,170 kilometres of roads,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-ar-1):14 and by 2014, more than 22,000 kilometers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-citizen-15)

SANRAL's operations are divided into two broad categories, namely toll roads, which are self-funding, and non-toll roads, which are funded by transfers from the Department of Transport. In 2014 toll roads constituted 14% (c. 3,000 km) of its responsibilities, and non-toll roads 86% (c. 19,000 km).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-citizen-15)

Some toll roads are concessions, privately funded and managed with supervision from SANRAL; these include the [Platinum Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_Highway "Platinum Highway") ([N1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N1_road_(South_Africa) "N1 road (South Africa)")/[N4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N4_road_(South_Africa) "N4 road (South Africa)")), the [Maputo Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maputo_Corridor "Maputo Corridor") (N4) and the [N3 Toll Concession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N3_(South_Africa)#N3_Toll_Concession "N3 (South Africa)").

Other toll roads are owned and operated directly by SANRAL; these include the [Huguenot Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot_Tunnel "Huguenot Tunnel") (N1), the [Tsitsikamma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsitsikamma "Tsitsikamma") Toll Road (N2), the [N2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N2_road_(South_Africa) "N2 road (South Africa)") tolls on the KwaZulu-Natal coast, the [Mariannhill Toll Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariannhill_Toll_Road "Mariannhill Toll Road") (N3), the N1 tolls in the Free State, Gauteng and Limpopo and the [N17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N17_(South_Africa) "N17 (South Africa)") tolls in Gauteng and Mpumalanga. It also owns and operates a tollgate on a provincial route (and not a national route), namely the Brandfort Toll Plaza on the R30 section of the [R30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R30_(South_Africa) "R30 (South Africa)")/[R730](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R730_(South_Africa) "R730 (South Africa)")/[R34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R34_(South_Africa) "R34 (South Africa)") ZR Mahabane Highway north of [Bloemfontein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloemfontein "Bloemfontein"). It also owns and operates the two tollgates on the [M4 freeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_(Pretoria) "M4 (Pretoria)") (Magalies Toll Route) west of Pretoria in Gauteng.

## Contributions to palaeontology and modern science

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=SANRAL&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Contributions to palaeontology and modern science")]

See also: [Waterloo Farm lagerstätte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterloo_Farm_lagerst%C3%A4tte "Waterloo Farm lagerstätte")

In the mid-1980s, a road bypass was constructed around Grahamstown (now [Makhanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makhanda,_Eastern_Cape "Makhanda, Eastern Cape")), to prevent traffic between [Port Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Elizabeth "Port Elizabeth") and [East London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London,_Eastern_Cape "East London, Eastern Cape") from driving through the [townships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Township_(South_Africa) "Township (South Africa)") following [Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") uprisings (which were progressively getting more heated at the time), making it unsafe for motorists.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_National_Roads_Agency#cite_note-16) In 1999 the newly constituted SANRAL tendered for upgrades of an unstable road cutting along this route. This road cutting contained an important 360 million year old fossil site previously researched by Robert W. Gess.

In 1999, SANRAL teamed up with Gess to assist with salvage blocks of a black shale from the cutting to prevent their loss to science. This and further salvage of shale blocks during further work on the cutting by SANRAL contractees in 2007–2008, and their subsequent ongoing excavation, led to the revelation of the now world renowned Waterloo Farm lagerstätte, the only estuarine fossil site in the world from about 360 million years ago, with exceptional soft-tissue preservation.

A few of the note-worthy fossils from Waterloo Farm include those of the first four-legged creatures (tetrapods) from Africa – _[Tutusius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutusius "Tutusius") umlambo_ and _[Umzantsia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umzantsia "Umzantsia") amazana_, as well as many other vertebrates such as Placodermi (e.g., _[Bothriolepis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bothriolepis "Bothriolepis") africana_; _[Groenlandaspis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groenlandaspis "Groenlandaspis") riniensi_), Acanthodii (e.g., _[Diplacanthus acus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplacanthus\_acus "Diplacanthus acus")_), Chondrichthyes (e.g., _[Antarctilamna ultima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctilamna\_ultima "Antarctilamna ultima")_), Actinopterygii and Sarcopterigii (e.g., _[Serenichthys kowiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenichthys\_kowiensis "Serenichthys kowiensis")_).

Agnatha included the worlds oldest fossil lamprey (_Priscomyzon riniensis_), the recently described juvenile which overturned our assumptions about vertebrates ancestry. The site has also revealed invertebrate remains including the scorpion _[Gondwanascorpio emzantsiensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwanascorpio\_emzantsiensis "Gondwanascorpio emzantsiensis")_, the oldest land animal from [Gondwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwana "Gondwana"), and a diverse flora of plants including _[Archaeopteris notosaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeopteris\_notosaria "Archaeopteris notosaria")_, Africa's earliest woody tree. In addition to numerus undescribed taxa and those currently being described (Housed at the Devonian Ecosystems Lab, Albany Museum, Makhanda), Gess and his team still has decade's worth of work ahead from the excavated blocks that were rescued from the road works with the help of SANRAL.

Ghana Highway Authority| Agency overview |
| --- |
| Formed | 1974 |
| Preceding agency | * Public Works Department |
| Headquarters | * [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") |
| Parent agency | [Ministry of Roads and Highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Roads_and_Highways_(Ghana) "Ministry of Roads and Highways (Ghana)") |

The **Ghana Highway Authority** (**GHA**) was established as a corporate body by GHA Degree 1974 (NRCD 298). NRCD 298 was repealed by the GHA Act 1997 (Act 540), which, however, continued the Authority in existence with responsibility for the administration, control, development, and maintenance of the [trunk road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trunk_road "Trunk road") network in [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"). This totals 13,367 km (8,306 mi) of highways and related facilities which make up about 33% of [Ghana's total road network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Road_Network "Ghana Road Network") of 40,186 km (24,970 mi) as of 2013.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-Ghana_Highways_Authority-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-2)

## Departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Departments")]

All the Divisions of the Authority are grouped under three main Departments, namely:

*   Administration Department
*   Development Department
*   Maintenance Department

## Administration Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Administration Department")]

This Department embraces 7 Divisions, namely:

*   Finance
*   Human Resource
*   Legal Service
*   Training & Development
*   Public Affairs
*   MIS Division

There is an Internal Audit Division, that is directly responsible to the Chief Executive but which for administration purposes, reports to the Deputy Chief Executive (Administration).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-3)

## Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development Department")]

This Department embraces 7 Divisions, namely:

*   Road Safety and Environment
*   Planning
*   Materials
*   Contracts
*   Quantity Surveying
*   Survey and Design
*   Bridges

The Head of this Department is the Deputy Chief Executive for Development.

## Maintenance Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Maintenance Department")]

This Department embraces:

*   Road Maintenance
*   Regional Offices (10 in all, one in each region)
*   Plant and Equipment

Ghana Highway Authority| Agency overview |
| --- |
| Formed | 1974 |
| Preceding agency | * Public Works Department |
| Headquarters | * [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") |
| Parent agency | [Ministry of Roads and Highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Roads_and_Highways_(Ghana) "Ministry of Roads and Highways (Ghana)") |

The **Ghana Highway Authority** (**GHA**) was established as a corporate body by GHA Degree 1974 (NRCD 298). NRCD 298 was repealed by the GHA Act 1997 (Act 540), which, however, continued the Authority in existence with responsibility for the administration, control, development, and maintenance of the [trunk road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trunk_road "Trunk road") network in [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"). This totals 13,367 km (8,306 mi) of highways and related facilities which make up about 33% of [Ghana's total road network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Road_Network "Ghana Road Network") of 40,186 km (24,970 mi) as of 2013.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-Ghana_Highways_Authority-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-2)

## Departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Departments")]

All the Divisions of the Authority are grouped under three main Departments, namely:

*   Administration Department
*   Development Department
*   Maintenance Department

## Administration Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Administration Department")]

This Department embraces 7 Divisions, namely:

*   Finance
*   Human Resource
*   Legal Service
*   Training & Development
*   Public Affairs
*   MIS Division

There is an Internal Audit Division, that is directly responsible to the Chief Executive but which for administration purposes, reports to the Deputy Chief Executive (Administration).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Highway_Authority#cite_note-3)

## Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development Department")]

This Department embraces 7 Divisions, namely:

*   Road Safety and Environment
*   Planning
*   Materials
*   Contracts
*   Quantity Surveying
*   Survey and Design
*   Bridges

The Head of this Department is the Deputy Chief Executive for Development.

## Maintenance Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ghana_Highways_Authority&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Maintenance Department")]

This Department embraces:

*   Road Maintenance
*   Regional Offices (10 in all, one in each region)
*   Plant and Equipment

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ghanaian abstract strategy game

For people named Oware, see [Oware (surname)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware_(surname) "Oware (surname)").

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Awale.jpg/250px-Awale.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Awale.jpg)

A game of _awale_

**Oware** is an [abstract strategy game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_strategy_game "Abstract strategy game") among the [mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala") family of board games (pit and pebble games) played worldwide with slight variations as to the layout of the game, number of players and strategy of play.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-1) Its origin is uncertain,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-2) but it is widely believed to be of [Ashanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_people "Ashanti people") origin.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-3)

Played in the [Bono Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_region "Bono region"), [Bono East Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_East_region "Bono East region"), [Ahafo Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahafo_Region "Ahafo Region"), [Central Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Region_(Ghana) "Central Region (Ghana)"), [Western Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Region_(Ghana) "Western Region (Ghana)"), [Eastern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Region_(Ghana) "Eastern Region (Ghana)"), and [Ashanti Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_Region "Ashanti Region") of [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-4) as well as throughout the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), oware and its variants have many names - **ayò**, **[ayoayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoayo "Ayoayo")** ([Yoruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_language "Yoruba language")), **awalé** ([Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast"), [Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin "Benin")), **wari** ([Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali")), **ouri, ouril or uril** ([Cape Verde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde")), **warri** (Caribbean), **wali** ([Dagbani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dagbani_language "Dagbani language")), **adji** ([Ewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewe_language "Ewe language")), **nchọ/ókwè** ([Igbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igbo_language "Igbo language")), **ise** ([Edo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_language "Edo language")), **awale** ([Ga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ga_language "Ga language")) (meaning "spoons" in English). A common name in English is **awari** but one of the earliest Western scholars to study the game, [Robert Sutherland Rattray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sutherland_Rattray "Robert Sutherland Rattray"), used the name _wari_.

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Rules")]

The following are the rules for the _abapa_ variation, considered to be the most appropriate for serious, adult play.

### Equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Equipment")]

The game requires an oware board and 48 seeds. A typical oware board has two straight rows of six pits, called "houses", and optionally one large "score" house at each end. Each player controls the six houses on their side of the board, and the score house on their end. The game begins with four seeds in each of the twelve smaller houses.

Boards may be elaborately carved or simple and functional; they may include a pedestal, or be hinged to fold lengthwise or crosswise and latch for portability and storage with the seeds inside. While most commonly located at either end, scoring houses may be placed elsewhere, and the rows do not need to be straight. When a board has a hinged cover like a [diptych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diptych "Diptych"), the scoring houses may be carved into the two halves of the cover, and so be in front of the players during play. The ground may also be used as a board; players simply scoop two rows of pits out of the earth.

In the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), the seeds are typically [nickernuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickernut "Nickernut"), which are smooth and shiny. Beads and pebbles are also sometimes used. In the West, some cheaper sets use oval-shaped [marbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marbles "Marbles"). Some tourist sets use [cowrie shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowrie_shell "Cowrie shell").

### Objective

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Objective")]

The game starts with four seeds in each house. The objective of the game is to capture more seeds than one's opponent. Since the game has only 48 seeds, capturing 25 is sufficient to win the game. Since there is an even number of seeds, it is possible for the game to end in a draw, where each player has captured 24.

### Sowing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Sowing")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Oware_09.jpg/330px-Oware_09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oware_09.jpg)

A player sowing seeds

Players take turns moving the seeds. On a turn, a player chooses one of the six houses under their control. The player removes all seeds from that house, and distributes them, dropping one in each house counter-clockwise from this house, in a process called _sowing_. Seeds are not distributed into the end scoring houses, nor into the house drawn from. The starting house is always left empty; if it contained 12 (or more) seeds, it is skipped, and the twelfth seed is placed in the next house. The diagram shows the result of sowing from house _E_.

Knowing the number of seeds in each house is, of course, important to game play. When there are many seeds in a house, sometimes enough to make a full lap of the board or more, they cannot easily be counted by eye, and their number is often guarded by the player who controls that house. This may be done by repeatedly moving the seeds in the house. A player may count the seeds when contemplating a move; in such cases the last few are usually counted in the hand to avoid revealing their number.

### Capturing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Capturing")]

In Oware Abapa, capturing occurs only when a player brings the count of an opponent's house to exactly two or three with the final seed they sowed in that turn.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-5) This always captures the seeds in the corresponding house, and possibly more: If the previous-to-last seed also brought an opponent's house to two or three, these are captured as well, and so on until a house is reached which does not contain two or three seeds or does not belong to the opponent. The captured seeds are placed in the player's scoring house (or set aside if the board has no scoring houses). However, if a move would capture all of an opponent's seeds, the capture is forfeited since this would prevent the opponent from continuing the game, and the seeds are instead left on the board. (However, see discussion on Grand Slam variations below). In the adjacent diagram, the lower player would capture all the seeds in houses _e_, _d_, and _c_ but not b (as it has four seeds) or _a_(since it is not contiguous to the other captured houses).

### Let the opponent play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Let the opponent play")]

The proscription against capturing all an opponent's seeds is related to a more general idea, that one ought to make a move that allows the opponent to continue playing. If an opponent's houses are all empty, the current player must make a move that gives the opponent seeds. If no such move is possible, the current player captures all seeds in their own territory, ending the game.

### Winning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Winning")]

The game is over when one player has captured 25 or more seeds, or each player has taken 24 seeds (draw). If both players agree that the game has been reduced to an endless cycle, the game ends when each player has seeds in their holes and then each player captures the seeds on their side of the board.

## Variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Variations")]

### "Grand slam" variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: \"Grand slam\" variations")]

A grand slam is capturing all of an opponent's seeds in one turn. There are variations to the rule that applies, which may be one of the following:[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-Grand_Slam_Variation-6)

1.   Grand slam captures are not legal moves.
2.   Such a move is legal, but no capture results. International competitions often follow this rule.
3.   Grand slam captures are allowed, however, all remaining stones on the board are awarded to the opponent.
4.   Such a move is legal, but the last (or first) house is not captured.

Various other rules also exist.

Variations allowing Grand slams to end the game are [strongly solved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solved_game "Solved game") by [Henri Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Bal "Henri Bal") and John Romein at the [Vrije Universiteit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrije_Universiteit "Vrije Universiteit") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") in 2002; either side can force a draw.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-Owari_is_Solved-7)

### Other

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Other")]

One commercial version was marketed in 1964 by 3M, as the board game _[Oh-Wah-Ree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh-Wah-Ree "Oh-Wah-Ree")_.

## History and society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: History and society")]

[![Image 59](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg/250px-Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg)

Awalé with the shape of an elephant

[![Image 60](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg/250px-Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg)

Weight for weighing gold dust – Awele or Awari game

Oware is perhaps the most widespread game in the [mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala") family of games.

Considered the national game of [Bono State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_state "Bono state"), [Ashanti City-State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_Region "Ashanti Region"), and [Antigua & Barbuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_and_Barbuda "Antigua and Barbuda"), oware is said to derive its name — which literally means "he/she marries" — from a legend in the [Akan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akan_language "Akan language") and [Twi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twi "Twi"), the language of the [Akan people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akan_people "Akan people"), about a man and a woman who played the game endlessly and, so as to be able to stay together and continue playing, they married.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-9)

Reflecting traditional African values, players of oware encourage participation by onlookers, making it perhaps the most social two-player abstract. In recreational play, it is normal for spectators to discuss the game in progress and to advise the players. Games may provide a focus for entertainment and meeting others. The game, or variations of it, also had an important role in teaching [arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic "Arithmetic") to African children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ghanaian abstract strategy game

For people named Oware, see [Oware (surname)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware_(surname) "Oware (surname)").

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Awale.jpg/250px-Awale.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Awale.jpg)

A game of _awale_

**Oware** is an [abstract strategy game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_strategy_game "Abstract strategy game") among the [mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala") family of board games (pit and pebble games) played worldwide with slight variations as to the layout of the game, number of players and strategy of play.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-1) Its origin is uncertain,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-2) but it is widely believed to be of [Ashanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_people "Ashanti people") origin.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-3)

Played in the [Bono Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_region "Bono region"), [Bono East Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_East_region "Bono East region"), [Ahafo Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahafo_Region "Ahafo Region"), [Central Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Region_(Ghana) "Central Region (Ghana)"), [Western Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Region_(Ghana) "Western Region (Ghana)"), [Eastern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Region_(Ghana) "Eastern Region (Ghana)"), and [Ashanti Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_Region "Ashanti Region") of [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-4) as well as throughout the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), oware and its variants have many names - **ayò**, **[ayoayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoayo "Ayoayo")** ([Yoruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_language "Yoruba language")), **awalé** ([Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast "Ivory Coast"), [Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin "Benin")), **wari** ([Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali "Mali")), **ouri, ouril or uril** ([Cape Verde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verde "Cape Verde")), **warri** (Caribbean), **wali** ([Dagbani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dagbani_language "Dagbani language")), **adji** ([Ewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewe_language "Ewe language")), **nchọ/ókwè** ([Igbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igbo_language "Igbo language")), **ise** ([Edo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_language "Edo language")), **awale** ([Ga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ga_language "Ga language")) (meaning "spoons" in English). A common name in English is **awari** but one of the earliest Western scholars to study the game, [Robert Sutherland Rattray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sutherland_Rattray "Robert Sutherland Rattray"), used the name _wari_.

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Rules")]

The following are the rules for the _abapa_ variation, considered to be the most appropriate for serious, adult play.

### Equipment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Equipment")]

The game requires an oware board and 48 seeds. A typical oware board has two straight rows of six pits, called "houses", and optionally one large "score" house at each end. Each player controls the six houses on their side of the board, and the score house on their end. The game begins with four seeds in each of the twelve smaller houses.

Boards may be elaborately carved or simple and functional; they may include a pedestal, or be hinged to fold lengthwise or crosswise and latch for portability and storage with the seeds inside. While most commonly located at either end, scoring houses may be placed elsewhere, and the rows do not need to be straight. When a board has a hinged cover like a [diptych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diptych "Diptych"), the scoring houses may be carved into the two halves of the cover, and so be in front of the players during play. The ground may also be used as a board; players simply scoop two rows of pits out of the earth.

In the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"), the seeds are typically [nickernuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickernut "Nickernut"), which are smooth and shiny. Beads and pebbles are also sometimes used. In the West, some cheaper sets use oval-shaped [marbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marbles "Marbles"). Some tourist sets use [cowrie shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowrie_shell "Cowrie shell").

### Objective

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Objective")]

The game starts with four seeds in each house. The objective of the game is to capture more seeds than one's opponent. Since the game has only 48 seeds, capturing 25 is sufficient to win the game. Since there is an even number of seeds, it is possible for the game to end in a draw, where each player has captured 24.

### Sowing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Sowing")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Oware_09.jpg/330px-Oware_09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oware_09.jpg)

A player sowing seeds

Players take turns moving the seeds. On a turn, a player chooses one of the six houses under their control. The player removes all seeds from that house, and distributes them, dropping one in each house counter-clockwise from this house, in a process called _sowing_. Seeds are not distributed into the end scoring houses, nor into the house drawn from. The starting house is always left empty; if it contained 12 (or more) seeds, it is skipped, and the twelfth seed is placed in the next house. The diagram shows the result of sowing from house _E_.

Knowing the number of seeds in each house is, of course, important to game play. When there are many seeds in a house, sometimes enough to make a full lap of the board or more, they cannot easily be counted by eye, and their number is often guarded by the player who controls that house. This may be done by repeatedly moving the seeds in the house. A player may count the seeds when contemplating a move; in such cases the last few are usually counted in the hand to avoid revealing their number.

### Capturing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Capturing")]

In Oware Abapa, capturing occurs only when a player brings the count of an opponent's house to exactly two or three with the final seed they sowed in that turn.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-5) This always captures the seeds in the corresponding house, and possibly more: If the previous-to-last seed also brought an opponent's house to two or three, these are captured as well, and so on until a house is reached which does not contain two or three seeds or does not belong to the opponent. The captured seeds are placed in the player's scoring house (or set aside if the board has no scoring houses). However, if a move would capture all of an opponent's seeds, the capture is forfeited since this would prevent the opponent from continuing the game, and the seeds are instead left on the board. (However, see discussion on Grand Slam variations below). In the adjacent diagram, the lower player would capture all the seeds in houses _e_, _d_, and _c_ but not b (as it has four seeds) or _a_(since it is not contiguous to the other captured houses).

### Let the opponent play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Let the opponent play")]

The proscription against capturing all an opponent's seeds is related to a more general idea, that one ought to make a move that allows the opponent to continue playing. If an opponent's houses are all empty, the current player must make a move that gives the opponent seeds. If no such move is possible, the current player captures all seeds in their own territory, ending the game.

### Winning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Winning")]

The game is over when one player has captured 25 or more seeds, or each player has taken 24 seeds (draw). If both players agree that the game has been reduced to an endless cycle, the game ends when each player has seeds in their holes and then each player captures the seeds on their side of the board.

## Variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Variations")]

### "Grand slam" variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: \"Grand slam\" variations")]

A grand slam is capturing all of an opponent's seeds in one turn. There are variations to the rule that applies, which may be one of the following:[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-Grand_Slam_Variation-6)

1.   Grand slam captures are not legal moves.
2.   Such a move is legal, but no capture results. International competitions often follow this rule.
3.   Grand slam captures are allowed, however, all remaining stones on the board are awarded to the opponent.
4.   Such a move is legal, but the last (or first) house is not captured.

Various other rules also exist.

Variations allowing Grand slams to end the game are [strongly solved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solved_game "Solved game") by [Henri Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Bal "Henri Bal") and John Romein at the [Vrije Universiteit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrije_Universiteit "Vrije Universiteit") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") in 2002; either side can force a draw.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-Owari_is_Solved-7)

### Other

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Other")]

One commercial version was marketed in 1964 by 3M, as the board game _[Oh-Wah-Ree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh-Wah-Ree "Oh-Wah-Ree")_.

## History and society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oware&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: History and society")]

[![Image 59](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg/250px-Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Awal%C3%A9_olifant.jpg)

Awalé with the shape of an elephant

[![Image 60](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg/250px-Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Akan_MHNT.ETH.2010.25.054.jpg)

Weight for weighing gold dust – Awele or Awari game

Oware is perhaps the most widespread game in the [mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala") family of games.

Considered the national game of [Bono State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_state "Bono state"), [Ashanti City-State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_Region "Ashanti Region"), and [Antigua & Barbuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigua_and_Barbuda "Antigua and Barbuda"), oware is said to derive its name — which literally means "he/she marries" — from a legend in the [Akan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akan_language "Akan language") and [Twi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twi "Twi"), the language of the [Akan people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akan_people "Akan people"), about a man and a woman who played the game endlessly and, so as to be able to stay together and continue playing, they married.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oware#cite_note-9)

Reflecting traditional African values, players of oware encourage participation by onlookers, making it perhaps the most social two-player abstract. In recreational play, it is normal for spectators to discuss the game in progress and to advise the players. Games may provide a focus for entertainment and meeting others. The game, or variations of it, also had an important role in teaching [arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic "Arithmetic") to African children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
